<meta>continues from previous page: not only confiscated the goods of individual citizens</meta> but also involved entire provinces and regions in a single type of calamity. Therefore, after foreign nations had been harassed and lost their sovereignty as an example to others, we saw Massilia <note>modern Marseille, a long-time ally of Rome that suffered under Julius Caesar</note> carried in a triumph. We saw a triumph celebrated over that city without which our commanders never celebrated a triumph from transalpine wars. I could mention many other wicked acts against our allies, if the sun had ever seen anything more unworthy than this one case. We are therefore punished by law. For unless we had borne their crimes unpunished, such unbridled license would never have reached a single man. From him, the inheritance of private property passed to a few, and the inheritance of ambition passed to many wicked men. Indeed, the seed and cause of civil wars will never be absent as long as desperate men remember that bloody spear and hope for it. When Lucius Sulla <note>Roman dictator who used public auctions, marked by a spear, to sell confiscated property</note> had brandished it while his kinsman was dictator, thirty-six years later he did not shrink from an even more criminal spear. Another, who had been a scribe in that first dictatorship, was the city quaestor in this one. From this, it should be understood that as long as such rewards are offered, civil wars will never cease. Thus, only the walls of the city stand and remain, and even these are now fearing the most extreme crimes. In truth, we have utterly lost the Republic. And we have fallen into these disasters. For we must return to our premise: while we were feared, we preferred to be loved. If such things could happen to the Roman people for ruling unjustly, what should individuals think? <insert>On how to obtain affection</insert>

But since it is clear that the power of goodwill is great, and that of fear is weak, it follows that we should discuss by what means we can most easily obtain that which we desire: honor, faith, and affection. But these are not equally

<summary>Cicero argues that Rome's decline and civil wars were caused by the shift from a protective empire to a cruel one that exploited its allies. He concludes that the power of goodwill is far superior to the instability of fear in maintaining authority.</summary>
